claims.claim: CORRECTED, the sweep WORST finding (F-FAIL, independently re-confirmed): the article called the enacting clause "a constitutional requirement that appears at the beginning of every federal law." It is STATUTORY. 1 U.S.C. 101 prescribes the wording and its own source note traces the requirement to an ordinary act of Congress - "(July 30, 1947, ch. 388, 61 Stat. 634.)". The page now quotes the section, quotes the source note, and states that the requirement is statutory rather than constitutional. The wording itself was already correct and is preserved. The 1 U.S.C. 102 resolving clause for joint resolutions is added alongside it.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): "It is important for citation purposes but doesn't do anything legally." Nothing stored settles the legal effect of a short-title section either way. The page now shows a real short-title section in full (H.R. 1011 sec. 1) and says only what it does - supplies the name by which the Act may be cited.

REMOVED, F-UNFETCHABLE (sweep) and re-confirmed unfetchable this session: "every bill introduced in Congress from the 93rd Congress (1973) forward, and partial records going back earlier." congress.gov/help/coverage-dates returns HTTP 403 even through the repo browser-UA path, so the claim cannot be sourced and is omitted rather than softened. The section now describes what each site is FOR, and anchors the enacted-text point on 1 U.S.C. 112 and 106a instead.

REMOVED, unsourced: "This is the version that was signed by the Speaker of the House, the President of the Senate, and the President of the United States. It's the law." Replaced with the statutory account of what is authoritative - the Statutes at Large under 1 U.S.C. 112, which "shall be legal evidence of laws", and the Archivist's custody of the originals under 1 U.S.C. 106a.

CLOSED, F-UNFETCHABLE (sweep): "The Congressional Record is published daily when Congress is in session" was flagged because the govinfo COLLECTION page renders as an empty JS shell. The stored capture data/ref-text/record-govinfo-crec-about.txt does carry the substantive text, and the sentence is now quoted from it verbatim, along with "The Congressional Record began publication in 1873, and is still published today."

REMOVED, S-RISK (sweep): "If a bill extends a surveillance authority to June 12, 2026, that date matters - it tells you when Congress will have to act again." The example was accurate at the May 2026 publication (119-S-4465 moved the FISA 702 repeal date to 2026-06-12) but that sunset has since passed, so a present-tense illustration of a future deadline had gone stale. Replaced with a dated provision that carries no currency claim: H.R. 1's "Effective Date.--The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025."

REMOVED, five U-FLAGs (sweep): "The formatting conventions have changed little in over a century"; "Most people never learn this structure, which is why most people rely on news summaries"; "This is where most readers get lost"; "Each section typically addresses a single subject"; and, on notwithstanding clauses, "These are often places where Congress is making a significant legal change" - the last also using a word SYSTEM_PROMPT RULE 7 bans outright. All rest on nothing stored. The notwithstanding passage now states the mechanical effect and quotes a real instance from H.R. 1.

REMOVED, unsourced editorial heuristic: "Look for the big numbers... A provision that appropriates $50 billion for defense is more significant than one that appropriates $2 million for a specific grant program." Both the ranking rule and the illustrative figures were invented. The section now offers three moves that are each demonstrable from the bill text itself.

ADDED, the sweep COVERAGE GAP: the guide never discussed findings sections, definitions sections, effective dates or severability - four parts a reader meets constantly. Each now has its own passage with a real example quoted from a stored 119th-Congress bill text (H.R. 1993 findings, H.R. 165 definitions, H.R. 1 effective date, H.R. 4371 severability). Also added: the House Rule XII clause 7(c)(1) constitutional authority statement, which is the first thing a House measure must produce and was absent from a guide about reading them.

RE-SOURCED: the four amendment formulas were previously illustrated with invented examples ("Section 1234(a) is amended by striking 2025 and inserting 2026"). All four are now quoted from ONE real stored bill text, H.R. 1 of the 119th Congress, and the U.S. Code cross-reference pattern is quoted from H.R. 1011 ("Section 401 of the Agricultural Credit Act of 1978 (16 U.S.C. 2201) is amended--"). The invented 42 U.S.C. 1395ww reference is gone.

SOURCING NOTE: CRS 98-265 was last updated July 17, 2003. It is used only for descriptive facts about the Record that the current GovInfo page does not state - the four sections, the H/S/E/D page prefixes, and the Daily Digest as index - and its date is given in the Key Sources box. The "published daily" currency claim is taken from the GovInfo capture, not from the 2003 report.

REMOVED, unsourced: the "revise and extend" paragraph asserting that members "can submit written statements that didn't occur verbatim on the floor and have them inserted into the Record as if they did" and that "A statement labeled EXTENSION OF REMARKS was submitted in writing, not spoken." Neither stored source states either proposition. What CRS does say about fidelity is quoted instead: the Record is "a substantially verbatim account ... subject only to technical, grammatical, and typographical corrections," and Extensions of Remarks is one of its four sections.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against data/bill-text/119-HR-4371.txt and CONFIRMED): the paragraph promised to show "what survives if a court strikes part of the Act" but the quote stopped before the word "severable" and before the survives / does-not-affect-the-remainder language. Quoted through the mechanism now. The doubled "the this" is the bill's own typo and is kept as printed, with a note on the page so a reader does not take it for a transcription error.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): the inserting-after example quoted only the bare section number "50924", so it demonstrated the formula without showing what was actually inserted. Extended to the full inserted item.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): the page stated as a general rule that the original of an enacted measure is received by the Archivist "from the President". 1 U.S.C. 106a carries a second pathway for a measure passed over a veto, where it comes instead from the President of the Senate or the Speaker. Both are now on the page.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): "it is a statutory requirement rather than a constitutional one" went one step past what the source affirmatively says - the 1947 source note establishes where the wording was enacted, not that no constitutional basis exists, and no constitutional text is among this ledger's sources. Reworded to what the source does establish: the requirement is written in statute, and the prescribed form is a creature of the U.S. Code rather than of a constitutional text. The sweep's underlying correction stands; only the inferential overreach is gone.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): "Before a House measure is introduced" generalised beyond Rule XII clause 7(c)(1), which reaches only a "bill or joint resolution" and not simple or concurrent resolutions. Scoped, with the limit stated on the page.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): the replacement for the removed Congress.gov coverage claim was itself untied to any stored source - it described what each website carries. Reduced to a bare orientation sentence, with the sourced statutory point (which text is authoritative once a measure is law) carrying the paragraph.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): "Three moves cover most of it" asserted real-world reading efficacy that no source supports - the same class the audit removed elsewhere on this page. Reworded to describe what the three moves are anchored in rather than how much they cover. The "worth reading... because it can carry real weight" gloss on definitions sections went with it.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): H.R. 165, H.R. 1993 and H.R. 4371 are quoted at length for the definitions, findings and severability examples but appeared in neither the Key Sources box nor the JSON-LD citation array, leaving a reader with no route to three of the five bill sources. Added to both.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NOTE): the inserted-text halves of the adding-at-the-end and inserting-after examples had no ledger rows of their own. The inserting-after item now has one; the adding-at-the-end item was already carried by an existing row.

ROUND 2, ACCEPTED AS IS (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NOTE): clause 7(c)(2), letting a committee chair submit the constitutional-authority statement for a SENATE bill or joint resolution, is not covered. The guide is framed around House-introduced measures and makes no completeness claim about the clause. Deliberate, recorded rather than silently left.

ROUND 2, ACCEPTED AS IS (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NOTE): this page quotes 1 U.S.C. 112 as "shall be legal evidence of laws", stopping before the rest of the list. Laws are this page's subject and nothing turns on the omitted items. The sibling bill-numbering page, where the public-law citation itself is the topic, quotes the sentence to its end.
The page covers where the enacting clause is prescribed

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): "in a long Act they are the fastest way to find the part you care about" survived the round-2 sweep of efficacy claims in the same three-move block. Reworded to "where to start".

ROUND 3, ACCEPTED AS IS (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NOTE): two H.R. 1 quotes drop the bill-drafting trailing "--" while a third keeps it. No word is altered in any of them and the "--" is a formatting convention rather than text; the inconsistency is cosmetic and the quotes remain verbatim substrings.

BATCH-WIDE SWEEP (2026-09-02), the systemic defect of this batch: 104 instances across all seven articles where a comma, period, semicolon or colon sat INSIDE a closing quotation mark although the source has no such character at that point. American typographic convention puts them there; this site rule does not allow it, because a span in quotation marks is a promise of verbatimness and invented punctuation inside the marks breaks that promise for a reader checking the source. Two hostile passes had each flagged one or two instances individually, which produced iterative one-at-a-time fixes and, on one span, three successive wrong repairs. The class was instead resolved MECHANICALLY: a scanner extracted every quoted span on every page, tested it against the concatenated registered sources for that article, and where the span matched only after stripping one trailing punctuation character, moved that character outside the closing quote. Per-article counts: what-is-a-committee 32, discharge-petition 22, house-rules-committee 19, bill-numbering 12, congressional-oversight 8, how-to-read-a-bill 7, joint-resolution 4. A re-scan after the sweep returns zero. No word in any quotation changed; only the position of punctuation relative to the closing mark.

SWEEP FOLLOW-UP, adjudicated not fixed: after the punctuation sweep the scanner still flags a handful of spans per page. Every one was inspected. They fall into three groups, none a defect. (1) Nested-quote renderings, where the source own internal quotation marks arrive as HTML entities or as double-backtick/double-apostrophe pairs and the page renders them as single quotes so they can sit inside a double-quoted span - already adjudicated per-article in earlier rounds. (2) Scanner pairing artefacts, where an odd number of quote characters in a paragraph makes the scanner slice across a boundary and produce a span that was never on the page. (3) The literal string article-body, which is the class attribute the scanner picks up when it strips tags. Recorded so a future audit running the same scanner does not re-open them.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 3, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against data/bill-text/119-HR-1.txt and CONFIRMED): the adding-at-the-end example quoted only the heading of the inserted subparagraph, so it showed the formula without showing that anything operative followed - the same defect the inserting-after example had been fixed for in round 2, left in place on its neighbour. Extended into the operative words.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 3, NON-BLOCKING): the clause saying a definitions section is worth reading before the operative sections was a residual reading-advice claim of the kind removed elsewhere on this page. Replaced with the structural reason a definitions section matters - its terms govern the operative sections that follow - which is what the quoted H.R. 165 span (In this Act:) actually establishes.

SWEEP CORRECTION (2026-09-02): the first quote-boundary sweep applied an outside-always rule, which was half right. The correct rule is two-sided - punctuation belongs INSIDE the closing quotation mark when the source sentence genuinely ends there, and OUTSIDE when the quote truncates mid-sentence. A second scanner was written to test both directions: for every quoted span it asks whether span+punctuation appears in the registered sources (then it belongs inside) or only span does (then outside). Across the seven articles it found 12 candidates for inside. Each was checked against the source bytes and only the genuine sentence-ends were moved: three on this batch (two on what-is-a-committee, one adjudicated the other way on house-rules-committee). The remaining nine were FALSE POSITIVES of the naive rule - semicolons and commas that are the page own list separators and merely happen to occur at the same point in the source. Those stay outside, because the punctuation is the article, not the quotation. The two already-published articles scanned clean in both directions.

MECHANICAL RETAG (2026-09-02): a hostile pass flagged three ledger rows typed "quote" whose prose actually paraphrases. Rather than fix three by hand, a detector compared every quote-typed row against the set of spans the page actually presents inside quotation marks. It found 84 such rows across the seven articles (house-rules-committee 21, how-to-read-a-bill 13, what-is-a-committee 12, congressional-oversight 10, discharge-petition 10, joint-resolution 9, bill-numbering 9) and retagged them "fact". The retag only weakens what the ledger claims about itself and never strengthens it; every receipt is unchanged and still verbatim. Same lesson as the punctuation class - a defect that recurs is cheaper to detect mechanically than to fix one instance at a time.

ROUND 4 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 4, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against data/bill-text/119-HR-1.txt and CONFIRMED): the striking-and-inserting example quoted only the bare subsection heading "(u) Thrifty Food Plan." - the third instance of the same defect on this page, after the inserting-after example in round 2 and the adding-at-the-end example in round 3. Extended into the operative definition. The heading period is part of the "Plan.--" separator, not a sentence end, so it stays where the source puts it.

ROUND 4 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 4, NON-BLOCKING): "and knowing them is most of the work" was a residual reading-efficacy claim of exactly the kind removed twice already on this page. Cut; the lede now says only what the guide covers.

ROUND 4 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 4, NON-BLOCKING): H.R. 1011 is quoted twice on the page (the short-title section and the U.S. Code cross-reference pattern) and appears in the Key Sources box, but was missing from the JSON-LD citation array. Added.
